That's not quite right, Riley — language models don't remember anything on their own. Each time you call the model, it starts completely fresh: no memory of yesterday, no memory of the last request, nothing, unless you explicitly hand it back in.

What actually happens *within* one conversation is that the whole chat history gets re-sent to the model every time — that's the context window, and it's what makes a single session feel like it "remembers" what you said five minutes ago. But once that conversation ends, it's gone. There's no little diary the model keeps between calls.

It's an easy mistake to make because talking to a chatbot feels continuous, like talking to a person. And some products (like ChatGPT's "memory" feature) *do* add persistent memory — but that's extra engineering bolted on by the app, not something the model does by itself.

Think of it like a line cook with zero memory between shifts. If a regular customer wants "the usual," the cook won't know that unless the restaurant writes it on an index card and hands it to the cook *before* they start cooking. The model is the cook; the card is memory you have to design and store yourself — in a database, a file, wherever — and then feed back into the prompt next time.

So for your makerspace assistant: if you want it to recall that a student finished laser-cutter training last week, you have to build that — store it somewhere, then look it up and insert it into the context at the start of the next conversation. That's a real design decision for your assistant, not something you get for free.

Quick check: if a student says "remind me what you told me yesterday," what does your assistant actually need in order to answer that correctly?
